sentences.text: Sylviornis neocaledoniae was a large, flightless bird that lived exclusively in New Caledonia within the Western Pacific. This species stood approximately 80 cm tall and had a body mass ranging from 27 to 34 kg.
Its anatomy featured a large skull with a high, laterally compressed beak topped by a bony knob, while its wings were reduced to small stubs.
The bird possessed unique skeletal features, including unfused clavicles, a high number of tail vertebrae, and a ribcage and pelvis resembling dinosaurs.
Sylviornis holds the record as the most massive pangalliform bird known to science.
Native accounts describe the bird as reddish with a star-shaped head marking, capable of running fast using its wings for balance.
Large tumuli on Île des Pins, initially thought to be graves, are hypothesized to be incubation mounds built by Sylviornis.
The genus Sylviornis was named by Poplin in 1980.
Thousands of subfossil bones of Sylviornis have been found on New Caledonia and the nearby Île des Pins.
The most recent fossil evidence of Sylviornis is a bone from the Pindai Caves dated to 1120–840 BCE.
Sylviornis likely had a well-developed sense of smell and was active during twilight hours.
Up to 50% of Sylviornis fossils found in some deposits belong to juvenile animals.
It is hypothesized that Sylviornis did not incubate its eggs but instead built large mounds similar to megapodes.
Native accounts state that Sylviornis laid a single egg between November and April without incubating or protecting it.
Adult Sylviornis were described as aggressive.
If native accounts are accurate, Sylviornis eggs and hatchlings would have been vulnerable to introduced mammalian predators.
The species of this extinct bird is Sylviornis neocaledoniae.
Sylviornis belongs to the extinct family Sylviornithidae and is related to the Galliformes group.
The parent group of the genus Sylviornis is the family Sylviornithidae.
Fossils of Sylviornis date to the Holocene epoch.
The time range for Sylviornis is the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
There is a debate over whether Sylviornis was a herbivore feeding on roots or a specialized invertebrate predator.
Recent assessments suggest it is unlikely that Sylviornis was a mound-builder because it is not closely related to megapodes.
